film.caption: Jasper Johns, 2:16. Tesa 41, October 2026
film.credit: Filmed by Bibiana Juritz and Aram Zadikian, edited by Bibiana Juritz. Sound on; captions in the player menu
p1: Every form in this work has its counterpart. A long plaster base, its face engraved with the name Jasper Johns, has a slot running along its top. Into the slot go slabs, upright, shoulder to shoulder, each a different colour: plaster cast with acrylic and pure pigment. Twelve pieces. On an afternoon at the end of October, in Tesa 41, Zadik and Aram Zadikian set them out on trestles against the brick wall and talked about what they were looking at. The film of that afternoon, Jasper Johns, is out today.
p2: Aram began with the base. “You have this base, and then you have these things that slot in. There’s something about this, almost like a sword in a sheath.” Slotting, he said, is a universal idea. And there is the name: the work is, in his words, an homage to Jasper Johns, to “the simplicity of a symbol” and to a form that holds something.
fig.name: The name on the bases
p3: Zadik went to the joint itself. “The connection between this and the bottom form: just perfect, like a handshake that people come up with instinctively.” Then, more widely: “In the universe, everything is fitting each other like this.” He went on to the body: the teeth in the gums, the head, all the forms fitting into one another and interweaving.
p4: It is also how the slabs are made. “You pour, just like this,” Zadik said of the slot: “this is almost like a mold. The liquid plaster goes in there; after thirty minutes you demold it. Then you get a piece from that cavity. It fits perfect.”
gal.zadik: Zadik setting slabs into a base
p5: Nothing in the work is glued or bolted. “Just like in life, nothing is fixed,” Zadik said. “This work is not fixed. All the elements can be moved and reshaped, and every time you move them around you come up with a completely new experience.”
p6: Aram heard in it what the studio has been finding all autumn: the power of repetition, “the simple loop repeated again and again, and suddenly you get a completely different experience.” And something about time. “There’s a rebirth in that process. Even this: we’ll never have this arrangement again.” Even putting a slab back exactly where it was, he pointed out, can’t be done to the millimetre. “There’s something that’s temporary about this work, and you’re embracing how temporary it is by not bolting anything together.”
p7: “There’s something reassuring when things fit together,” Aram said. “We want things to fit together.” Then they took the twelve apart again, one by one.
